1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. MSK: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka; DMS: Database Migration Service; ETL: extract, transform, load; SDK: software development kit; SQS: Simple Queue Service; SNS: Simple Notification Service; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud

  • Read data from streaming sources: Amazon Kinesis, Amazon MSK, DynamoDB Streams, AWS DMS, AWS Glue and Amazon Redshift
  • Choose between Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose and Amazon MSK
  • Call a Lambda function from Kinesis and tune batches, errors and parallelism
  • Manage fan-in and fan-out of streaming data
  • Describe replayability of an ingestion pipeline
  • Tell stateful from stateless processing

2Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits

Running case

Kestrel Freight Tracks Its Trucks

  • 2,000 trucks send a position and temperature reading every few seconds
  • Dispatchers need the map to update within seconds
  • The analytics team wants every reading in S3, in a query-friendly format
  • If a processing bug is found, they must be able to replay the last two days
  • Your job: choose the streaming services and set them up

Service What it is Pick it when
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams A managed, durable, ordered stream split into shards; you write the consumers You need custom processing, several consumers, replay and second-level latency
Amazon Data Firehose [Old name: Kinesis Data Firehose] A managed delivery service with buffering, optional transformation and format conversion You only need to load streaming data into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, Apache Iceberg tables or an HTTP endpoint with no code
Amazon MSK Managed Apache Kafka: brokers, topics, partitions, consumer groups You already use Kafka or need the Kafka protocol and ecosystem
DynamoDB Streams An ordered log of item changes in one table, kept 24 hours You must react to changes in a DynamoDB table
AWS DMS (CDC) Reads a database's change log and writes the changes to a target (S3, Kinesis, Kafka and more) You must stream database changes without touching the application
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Managed Apache Flink for stateful stream processing Windows, joins and aggregations over a stream
AWS Glue streaming jobs Spark Structured Streaming ETL that reads Kinesis or Kafka Serverless stream ETL into S3 or other stores
Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion A materialized view reads straight from Kinesis or MSK Low-latency analytics in the warehouse with no staging in S3
Exam tip

Kinesis Data Streams = you build and read the stream; Data Firehose = it delivers for you. If the question says replay, multiple consumers or custom logic, it is Data Streams (or MSK). If it says load into S3 or Redshift with no administration, it is Firehose.

3Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

How it works

  • A stream has one or more shards; a record carries a partition key, a data blob and a sequence number
  • The partition key is hashed to choose the shard: the same key goes to the same shard, so order is kept per key (not across the whole stream)
  • Producers: PutRecord / PutRecords (up to 500 records per call), the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) (batches and aggregates), the Kinesis Agent (files and logs), AWS SDKs, IoT and other AWS services
  • Consumers: the Kinesis Client Library (KCL) (tracks progress with checkpoints), AWS Lambda, Amazon Data Firehose, Managed Service for Apache Flink, AWS Glue, your own code

Capacity modes and limits [Verify live]

Mode You manage Throughput
On-demand Nothing: shards scale automatically New streams start at 4 MB/s write and 8 MB/s read and scale up (up to 10 GB/s write in the largest Regions)
Provisioned The number of shards (change with UpdateShardCount, split and merge) Each shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write; 2 MB/s read
  • Record size: up to 10 MiB before base64 encoding (older material says 1 MB), designed for occasional large records
  • Retention: 24 hours by default, configurable from 24 hours up to 365 days
  • Reading: each shard allows 5 GetRecords calls per second and 2 MB/s shared by all standard consumers
  • Throttling: writing above the shard limit raises ProvisionedThroughputExceededException; fix with more shards, a better partition key, batching and backoff

Hot shards

  • A hot shard gets more traffic than its limit because many records share one partition key (for example one very busy truck or a constant key)
  • Fix: use a key with many distinct values (truck ID plus a small random suffix), split the hot shard, or use on-demand mode
Exam tip

"Records for the same device must stay in order" → use the device ID as the partition key. "One shard is throttled while others are idle" → a hot partition key.

4Amazon Data Firehose [Old name: Kinesis Data Firehose]

  • A fully managed delivery service: no shards to manage, it scales automatically
  • Sources: direct PUT from producers, a Kinesis data stream, MSK, CloudWatch Logs and events, IoT and more
  • Destinations: Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift (loads through S3 with a COPY command), Amazon OpenSearch Service, Splunk, Apache Iceberg tables, HTTP endpoints and partner services
  • Near real time: it buffers by size and time and delivers when either is reached first (S3 default: 5 MiB or 300 seconds; the interval can be set from 0 to 900 seconds; zero buffering trades more small objects for lower latency) [Verify live]
  • Optional features: a Lambda transformation, format conversion to Parquet or ORC (uses a schema from the Glue Data Catalog), dynamic partitioning (S3 prefixes by record fields), source-record backup to another S3 bucket
  • A record can be as large as 1,000 KB
  • Not a store: Firehose cannot replay; keep a Kinesis stream or an S3 backup if you need replay
Exam tip

"Deliver streaming logs to S3 as Parquet, partitioned by date, with no servers" → Data Firehose with format conversion and dynamic partitioning.

5Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)

  • Fully managed Apache Kafka: AWS runs the brokers (at least one per Availability Zone) and the controllers, and replaces failed brokers; existing Kafka clients and tools work unchanged
  • Concepts: topics are split into partitions; producers write, consumer groups read; each partition is read by one consumer per group
  • Cluster types: MSK Provisioned (Standard or Express brokers: you choose broker count and size) and MSK Serverless (no capacity to manage)
  • MSK Connect runs Kafka Connect connectors to stream data to and from other systems; MSK Replicator copies data between clusters
  • Retention is set per topic (not fixed at 24 hours); Kafka suits long retention and replay by offset
Kinesis Data Streams Amazon MSK
Model AWS-native streams and shards Kafka topics and partitions
Pick when Simplest AWS integration, on-demand scaling Existing Kafka apps, Kafka ecosystem, larger messages and long retention control
Capacity On-demand or shards Brokers (Provisioned) or Serverless
Exam tip

"Migrate an on-premises Kafka application with no code changes" → Amazon MSK.

6DynamoDB Streams, DMS and Other Streaming Reads

DynamoDB Streams (skill 1.1.1)

  • Records item-level changes (create, update, delete) in order, kept for 24 hours; each stream record appears exactly once, and order is kept per item
  • View types: keys only, new image, old image, new and old images; the type cannot be edited after the stream is set up
  • Typical use: a Lambda trigger that replicates, audits or enriches changes; a Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB integration is the choice for longer retention and more consumers
  • Enabling a stream has no performance impact on the table

AWS DMS, Glue and Redshift as streaming sources

  • AWS DMS reads the transaction log of a source database and streams ongoing changes to targets such as Kinesis Data Streams, Kafka, S3 and Redshift
  • AWS Glue streaming jobs read Kinesis or Kafka, process micro-batches with Spark Structured Streaming, and write to S3 and other stores; they checkpoint progress
  • Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion reads from Kinesis or MSK into a materialized view that refreshes continuously

7Calling a Lambda Function from Kinesis (skill 1.1.7)

  • You connect Lambda to a stream with an event source mapping: Lambda polls each shard and invokes your function with a batch of records from one shard
  • Standard consumer: shares the shard's 2 MB/s with other consumers. Enhanced fan-out consumer: a dedicated connection per shard, lower latency
  • Batch size and batching window: by default Lambda invokes as soon as records are available; a batching window of up to 5 minutes collects larger batches; the batch is also capped at 6 MB
  • Parallelization factor (1 to 10): several concurrent batches per shard; order is still kept per partition key
  • Errors: Lambda retries the failing batch and blocks that shard until it succeeds or the record expires; use bisect batch on function error, maximum retry attempts, maximum record age and an on-failure destination (SQS, SNS) so one bad record does not stop the stream
  • Processing is at least once: make the function idempotent
  • Tumbling windows let a function aggregate records over a time window
  • To go faster: add shards, raise the parallelization factor, use enhanced fan-out, or reserve concurrency
Exam tip

"A poison record blocks a shard and the iterator age rises" → bisect on error, limit retries and record age, and send failures to an on-failure destination.

8Fan-In and Fan-Out (skill 1.1.10)

Pattern Meaning How
Fan-in Many producers → one stream Every producer calls PutRecord or uses the KPL (batching, aggregation); the partition key spreads the load; Firehose or MSK accept many senders
Fan-out (shared) Several consumers read the same stream Standard consumers share 2 MB/s per shard and 5 reads per second: more consumers means throttling and delay
Fan-out (enhanced) Each consumer gets its own 2 MB/s per shard Enhanced fan-out (RegisterStreamConsumer): up to 20 registered consumers per stream (50 with on-demand advantage) [Verify live]; HTTP/2 push, lower latency, extra cost
Fan-out by messaging One event to many subscribers SNS topic with SQS queues, or EventBridge rules
Kafka Many consumer groups read the same topic independently Each consumer group keeps its own offset
Exam tip

"Five applications read the same stream and throttle each other" → enhanced fan-out.

9Replayability (skill 1.1.11)

  • Replayability is the ability to re-run ingestion over past data after a bug, a schema change or a new consumer
  • Where the history lives: Kinesis (retention 24 hours up to 365 days), MSK (per-topic retention and offsets), S3 (a raw zone that keeps every record), DynamoDB Streams (24 hours only)
  • How to replay: start a consumer from the oldest record (TRIM_HORIZON) or a timestamp (AT_TIMESTAMP), reset the Kafka offsets, rewind a Glue job bookmark, or redrive an SQS dead-letter queue
  • Design for it: keep raw data unchanged, make transformations idempotent (the same input gives the same output, no duplicates), use unique record IDs or upserts, and write results to a new location or overwrite whole partitions
  • Firehose keeps no history: enable source record backup to S3 if you need it
Exam tip

"Reprocess the last 48 hours after a bug fix" → a stream with at least 48 hours of retention (or raw data in S3) plus idempotent consumers.

10Stateful and Stateless Data Transactions (skill 1.1.12)

  • Stateless: each record is processed on its own, with no memory of earlier records (filter, map, convert format, enrich with a lookup). Easy to scale and retry
  • Stateful: the result depends on earlier records: windows, running totals, joins, sessionization, de-duplication. The engine must keep state and checkpoint it
  • Services for stateful work: Managed Service for Apache Flink (state and checkpoints), Spark Structured Streaming in Glue or EMR, Lambda tumbling windows (small cases)
  • Window types: tumbling (fixed, no overlap), sliding (overlapping), session (gap-based)
  • Stateful data transactions (a multi-step operation that must remember where it is) need a state store or checkpoint; stateless transactions carry everything in the request
Exam tip

"Count events per truck in 5-minute windows" is stateful → Flink or Spark Structured Streaming. "Convert each record's timestamp format" is stateless → Lambda or Firehose transformation.

11Exam Q&A

11.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Kestrel Freight wants every truck reading delivered to Amazon S3 as Parquet files partitioned by date, with no servers to manage and no custom consumer code. Which service should the data engineer use?

  • AAmazon Data Firehose with format conversion and dynamic partitioning
  • BAmazon Kinesis Data Streams with a custom Kinesis Client Library application
  • CAmazon MSK with a Kafka consumer running on Amazon EC2 instances
  • DDynamoDB Streams with an AWS Lambda function that writes the files
Show the answer

Answer: A. Amazon Data Firehose delivers streaming data to S3 without servers, can convert to Parquet and can partition by record fields. The others require you to build and run consumers.

S2Records for each truck must be processed in order, and traffic is spread evenly across thousands of trucks. How should the producer choose the partition key for Kinesis Data Streams?

  • AUse a constant value for every record
  • BUse the truck ID
  • CUse the current time
  • DUse a random number
Show the answer

Answer: B. Records with the same partition key go to the same shard and stay in order, and thousands of distinct truck IDs spread the load. A constant key creates a hot shard; random values break per-truck order.

S3Four applications read the same Kinesis data stream and the consumers are slowed by throttling on the shared read throughput. What is the best way to fix this?

  • AIncrease the retention period of the stream to seven days
  • BSwitch the producer from PutRecords to PutRecord for every record
  • CConvert the stream to Amazon Data Firehose with a larger buffer
  • DRegister the consumers for enhanced fan-out
Show the answer

Answer: D. Standard consumers share 2 MB/s per shard; enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard.

S4A Lambda function reads from a Kinesis data stream. One malformed record makes the function fail every time, and the stream's iterator age keeps growing. Which TWO settings help the stream keep moving? (Select TWO.)

  • AIncrease the shard count only
  • BConfigure an on-failure destination and limit maximum retry attempts or record age
  • CEnable bisect batch on function error
  • DSet the batching window to 0 seconds
  • EDisable the event source mapping permanently
Show the answer

Answer: B, C. Bisecting the batch isolates the bad record, and an on-failure destination with retry and age limits stops one record from blocking the shard. More shards do not remove a poison record, and disabling the mapping stops all processing.

S5A team must reprocess the last 48 hours of events after fixing a bug in a consumer. The events are in a Kinesis data stream with the default retention. What should the engineer do?

  • ADo nothing, because the stream still holds the last 48 hours of data by default retention settings
  • BEnable Amazon Data Firehose backup on the stream and replay from the backup
  • CCreate a new DynamoDB table and copy the shard iterators into it
  • DIncrease the retention period before the data ages out, then replay from a timestamp
Show the answer

Answer: D. The default retention is 24 hours, so older data is already gone for a 48-hour replay; extend retention (up to 365 days) and read from the oldest record or a timestamp. Keeping raw data in S3 is the longer-term answer.

S6An existing on-premises Apache Kafka application must move to AWS with minimal code changes. Which service fits best?

  • AAmazon Kinesis Data Streams
  • BAmazon SQS
  • CAmazon EventBridge
  • DAmazon MSK
Show the answer

Answer: D. Amazon MSK runs open-source Apache Kafka, so existing clients and tools work without changes.

S7Which workload is stateful?

  • AConverting each record's timestamp to UTC before it is stored
  • BDropping the records where the temperature field is empty
  • CAdding a customer name from a lookup table to each record as it arrives
  • DCounting events per truck in a rolling five-minute window
Show the answer

Answer: D. A windowed count depends on earlier records and needs state and checkpoints. The other tasks treat each record independently.

12Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Kinesis Data Streams Shards; partition key → shard → order per key; write 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s per shard, read 2 MB/s shared; retention 24 h to 365 days; on-demand or provisioned
Data Firehose Delivery, no replay; S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, Iceberg, HTTP; buffer size or time; Lambda transform; Parquet/ORC; dynamic partitioning
MSK Managed Kafka; topics, partitions, consumer groups; Provisioned or Serverless; MSK Connect; per-topic retention
DynamoDB Streams Item changes, 24 hours, exactly once, ordered per item; 4 view types
DMS CDC Streams database changes to Kinesis, Kafka, S3
Lambda + Kinesis Event source mapping; batch from one shard; batching window up to 5 min; parallelization 1–10; bisect, retries, on-failure destination; at least once
Fan-out Shared 2 MB/s per shard; enhanced fan-out = own 2 MB/s per consumer (20 consumers)
Replay Retention + TRIM_HORIZON / AT_TIMESTAMP; raw data in S3; idempotent consumers
Stateful Windows, joins, aggregates: Flink or Spark Structured Streaming; stateless: filter, map, convert
